content.question: What is a good indicator of economic development?
content.note: A Steady Growth in GDP (Gross Domestic Product) is considered a reliable indicator of economic development as it signifies an increase in the production of goods and services over time.

content.question: What was the male literacy rate as per Census 2011?
content.note: Per the Census 2011, the male literacy rate in India was 82.14%, significantly higher than the female literacy rate (65.46%).

content.question: Which state has the lowest poverty ratio as per NITI Aayog MPI 2021?
content.note: As per the NITI Aayog MPI 2021, Kerala recorded the lowest percentage of poverty in the country, showcasing high social development.

content.question: Which state had a population density of 17 persons per sq km in 2011?
content.note: Arunachal Pradesh had the lowest population density in 2011 with only 17 persons per sq km, due to its mountainous terrain and large forest cover.

content.question: Which committee was formed to assess poverty in India?
content.note: The Suresh Tendulkar Committee (2009) was constituted to review the methodology for poverty estimation in India, moving away from just calorie intake to include health and education.

content.question: What is a closed economy?
content.answer: An economy with no flow of labour, goods, and money with other countries
content.note: A Closed Economy is one that does not engage in international trade (imports/exports) or financial transfers with the rest of the world. It is self-sufficient.

content.question: What is meant by red tape in an economy?
content.note: Red Tape refers to excessive bureaucracy or rigid adherence to formal rules and regulations that are considered redundant and hinder decision-making.

content.question: What is the reverse repo rate?
content.answer: Interest rate at which RBI absorbs liquidity from banks
content.note: The Reverse Repo Rate is the rate at which the RBI borrows money from commercial banks. Increasing this rate helps the RBI suck out excess liquidity from the banking system.

content.question: What is fiscal deficit?
content.answer: Excess of government expenditure over revenue excluding borrowings
content.note: Fiscal Deficit is the difference between the government’s total expenditure and its total receipts (excluding borrowings). It indicates how much the government needs to borrow.

content.question: What is bank rate?
content.answer: Rate at which commercial banks borrow from RBI
content.note: The Bank Rate is the official interest rate at which the central bank (RBI) lends money to domestic banks, usually in the form of very short-term loans.

content.question: What was the urban population percentage in India as per Census 2011?
content.note: According to Census 2011, 31.16% of India's population lived in urban areas, while 68.84% lived in rural areas.

content.question: Agricultural equipment manufacturing belongs to which sector?
content.note: Manufacturing Agricultural Equipment is part of the Secondary Sector because it involves industrial processing and the creation of capital goods.

content.question: Which Union Territory has the lowest population density?
content.note: Among Union Territories, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands have the lowest population density (approx 46 per sq km) due to their geographic isolation.

content.question: PM SVANidhi scheme is for which group?
content.note: The PM SVANidhi (Street Vendor’s AtmaNirbhar Nidhi) scheme was launched to provide affordable working capital loans to street vendors to resume livelihoods post-COVID-19 lockdowns.

content.question: What represents the standard of living in a country?
content.note: Per Capita Income (Average Income) is used as a proxy for the Standard of Living. It is calculated by dividing the National Income by the total population.

content.question: Which country was a centrally planned economy in the 20th century?
content.note: The Soviet Union (USSR) was the most prominent example of a Centrally Planned Economy, where the state made all decisions regarding production and distribution.

content.question: If the price of a cheap good falls, what happens to its demand?
content.note: For most goods, the Law of Demand applies: when the price falls, the quantity demanded increases. (Note: For Giffen goods, this may differ).

content.question: What was the Bombay Plan?
content.answer: A plan of economic development formulated in 1944 by Indian capitalists
content.note: The Bombay Plan was a set of proposals for the post-WWII development of the Indian economy, published in 1944 by eight leading Indian industrialists.

content.question: Why is India called a mixed economy?
content.answer: Because private and public sectors coexist
content.note: India is a Mixed Economy because it follows a 'middle path' where the Private Sector (market mechanism) and Public Sector (state planning) work together.

content.question: Under which system does RBI issue currency?
content.note: The RBI follows the Minimum Reserve System for issuing currency notes. It must maintain a minimum reserve of ₹200 crores (115 in gold, 85 in foreign securities).

content.question: What causes inflation?
content.answer: Increase in money supply and decrease in production
content.note: Inflation occurs when there is too much money chasing too few goods. It is characterized by a general increase in prices and a fall in the purchasing value of money.

content.question: Mahalanobis model is related to which plan?
content.note: The Second Five Year Plan (1956-1961) was based on the P.C. Mahalanobis Model, which emphasized rapid industrialization with a focus on heavy industries.

content.question: When did the First Five Year Plan start?
content.note: The First Five Year Plan was launched in 1951 and focused primarily on the development of the Agricultural Sector to ensure food security.

content.question: What was the aim of the Twelfth Five Year Plan?
content.note: The core objective of the Twelfth Plan was 'Faster, More Inclusive and Sustainable Growth', emphasizing environmental protection and poverty reduction.

content.question: What are Open Market Operations?
content.answer: Buying and selling of government securities by RBI
content.note: Open Market Operations (OMO) involve the buying and selling of G-Secs (Government Securities) by the RBI to regulate the money supply in the economy.

content.question: Which state set up District Investment Promotion Agencies (DIPA)?
content.note: Odisha is the first state in India to constitute District Investment Promotion Agencies (DIPA) to facilitate investments at the district level.

content.question: Which state has the second largest population after Uttar Pradesh?
content.note: Maharashtra is the second most populous state in India. Uttar Pradesh holds the first rank.

content.question: What is globalisation?
content.answer: Integration of domestic economy with global economy
content.note: Globalisation is the process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries through trade, investment, and technology.

content.question: Which sector converts primary materials into finished goods?
content.note: The Secondary Sector (Industrial Sector) is responsible for processing raw materials into finished goods, adding value to the primary products.

content.question: Which is not part of the primary sector?
content.note: Bank Services are part of the Tertiary (Service) Sector. The primary sector only includes activities like farming, mining, and fishing.

content.question: Speculative demand for cash depends on what?
content.note: According to Keynes, the Speculative Demand for Money is highly sensitive to changes in interest rates. People hold cash to take advantage of future interest rate changes.

content.question: What is the law of increasing returns associated with?
content.note: The Law of Increasing Returns implies that as production expands, efficiency increases, which leads to a Decreasing Cost per unit of output.

content.question: When demand curve shifts right at same price, what happens to quantity demanded?
content.note: A Rightward Shift in the demand curve (at the same price) represents an increase in demand due to external factors like income rise or change in taste.

content.question: Why do diamonds cost more than water?
content.note: This is the Diamond-Water Paradox. Diamonds are expensive because their Marginal Utility (utility of the last unit) is high due to scarcity, whereas water has high total utility but low marginal utility.

content.question: Which is an example of the primary sector?
content.note: Forestry involves the collection and management of natural resources directly from the environment, making it a classic example of the Primary Sector.

content.question: Into how many sectors are economic activities divided?
content.note: Economic activities are traditionally divided into Three Sectors: Primary (extraction), Secondary (manufacturing), and Tertiary (services).

content.question: What are the components of basic social infrastructure?
content.note: Social Infrastructure includes the basic facilities that improve the quality of human life, specifically Education, Health, and Housing/Sanitation.

content.question: In which system does government decide production based on needs?
content.note: In a Socialist System (Command Economy), the Central Authority or Government plans and decides what to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce.

content.question: In socialism, how are goods distributed?
content.note: Socialism emphasizes Equity. Therefore, goods and services are distributed based on the actual needs of the people rather than their ability to pay.

content.question: What is a capitalist economy?
content.answer: Private ownership with production based on demand and supply
content.note: A Capitalist Economy (Market Economy) is characterized by private ownership of the means of production and minimal government intervention.

content.question: In a capitalist economy, prices are determined by what?
content.note:
In capitalism, the Price Mechanism (the 'Invisible Hand') determines prices through the forces of demand and supply in the free market.
Real-life Example: During a sudden rainstorm, the price of umbrellas at a street corner goes up because demand is high and supply is limited. That's capitalism.

content.question: Who gave the Ability Principle of Taxation?
content.note: The Ability to Pay Principle suggests that those who have more resources/income should pay more in taxes. It was advocated by Adam Smith as a canon of taxation.

content.question: Which sector is also called the service sector?
content.note:
The Tertiary Sector is known as the Service Sector because it provides support services to the primary and secondary sectors rather than producing tangible goods.
Real-life Example: When you go to a hospital or use Amazon to deliver a package, you are consuming services. These businesses don't 'grow' or 'manufacture' the product; they provide the expertise or logistics.

content.question: How is net investment calculated?
content.note:
Net Investment is calculated as Gross Investment - Depreciation. Depreciation represents the wear and tear of capital assets over time.
Real-life Example: If a delivery company buys 10 new bikes (Gross Investment) but 2 old bikes break down and are scrapped (Depreciation), the Net Investment is only 8 bikes.

content.question: Which institution is responsible for calculating India's GDP?
content.note:
The Central Statistical Institute (CSO), now part of the National Statistical Office (NSO), is the nodal agency responsible for coordinating statistical activities and calculating the Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
Think of the CSO as the 'Chief Accountant' of India. They gather data from shops, factories, and farms to announce if the 'Business of India' is growing or shrinking.

content.question: What was the duration of the Twelfth Five Year Plan?
content.note: The Twelfth Five Year Plan was the last formal five-year plan in India, spanning from 2012 to 2017. It was later replaced by NITI Aayog's three-year action agendas.

content.question: According to Census 2011, which state has the lowest literacy rate?
content.note: Based on Census 2011, Bihar recorded the lowest literacy rate in the country at approximately 61.8%.

content.question: According to Census 2011, which state has the lowest sex ratio?
content.note: Sex Ratio is defined as the number of females per 1,000 males. Haryana has the lowest ratio (879) among Indian states as per the 2011 Census.
